Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

The event happened because of the way I acted

vignette:
Maren Kowalski is a 26-year-old single woman of Polish-American descent who works as a firefighter with a municipal department in the Pacific Northwest. She presented for psychological assessment approximately four months after being held captive for just under three days following a structural collapse during a warehouse fire. While attempting to locate a missing crew member in a section of the building that had been cleared for entry, a secondary ceiling collapse trapped Maren in a confined storage room with no radio contact and no visible exit. She was found alive on the third day, dehydrated and with a fractured wrist, after a coordinated search located her position. The room in which she was held was small, dark, and filled with industrial shelving that had partially collapsed around her. She had been unable to stand for most of her captivity, wedged into a corner, and the only light available had come through a narrow gap near the floor that had slowly darkened and brightened with each passing day.

In the weeks that followed her rescue, Maren noticed that the world had changed in ways she struggled to name. She returned to modified duty after her wrist healed, but the firehouse - a place she had loved - had become difficult to inhabit. When the crew gathered in the common room after a call, the noise and press of bodies around her produced a sharpening sensation she could not will away, a physical alertness that made her want to find a wall and put her back against it. She had come to believe that crowded spaces were, in some fundamental way, threatening, even when she could see plainly that nothing was wrong. Ordinary sounds - a cabinet slamming, a radio crackling to life, a colleague dropping a tool on the concrete floor - made her flinch visibly, and she was certain that her crewmates had begun to notice. She was unable to settle in the evenings, lying awake in her apartment with the lights on, her body refusing the signal that she was safe.

What frightened her most, in a quiet and persistent way, was what had happened to her memory. The three days in that room did not feel like something that had happened to her - they felt, as she described it, like watching footage of a stranger. And yet at the same time, specific moments from the captivity arrived with a sharpness that her ordinary memories never had: the exact texture of the concrete floor, the particular quality of silence between the sounds of the structure settling. Remembering was less like recollection and more like being handed a photograph - precise, flat, and immediate. These images came without invitation. She might be writing a report at her station desk and find herself, without transition, back in the corner of that room, not as a memory but as a present fact.

She had stopped keeping photos on her phone from before the incident. A colleague had shared a group picture from a department event the previous summer, and seeing her own face from that time - open, unguarded - had produced a wave of disorientation so acute she had excused herself from the room. She had come to feel that the woman in those images was someone she no longer had access to, and she was not sure she would be able to find her way back. She had told herself, and continued to believe despite the evidence of the collapse report, that she had made a wrong decision about where to position herself that morning - that if she had moved differently, chosen differently, she would not have been in that room at all. This belief sat in her like a stone.

Over the following months, she had declined invitations, avoided the grocery store on weekends, and had not attended her department's monthly social gathering since the incident. A friendship with another firefighter, someone she had been close to for two years, had quietly dissolved because she had stopped returning calls.

She came to therapy at the suggestion of her department's peer support coordinator, after a flashback during a routine training exercise left her standing outside the building unable to re-enter. What she hoped for, she said carefully, was to feel like herself again. What she feared most was that there was no longer a self to return to.
